opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the single most important thing is that your experiments should actually be capable of telling you that you're wrong. It sounds obvious, but a lot of research, and honestly a lot of my own early research, involves running experiments that would look kind of fine no matter what was true about the world. You get some nice-looking plot, it's consistent with your hypothesis, and you feel great. But if you'd asked yourself beforehand, "What would this plot look like if my hypothesis were false?", the answer would often be: basically the same.

So the first thing I try to get people to do is be really explicit about what they believe and what evidence would change their mind. Then design the experiment that most cleanly distinguishes between the hypotheses you actually care about, rather than the one that's easiest to run or produces the prettiest figure.

The second thing is baselines and sanity checks. Especially in interpretability, it's incredibly easy to fool yourself. You find some direction in activation space that seems to represent a concept, and it's really exciting, but then you check whether a random direction would've done just as well, or whether a simpler explanation like "it's just detecting this token" accounts for everything, and the effect evaporates. I think a good set of experiments has a lot of these boring checks built in, and a good researcher is genuinely trying to kill their own hypothesis rather than defend it.

Third, I'd say convergent evidence. Any single technique has failure modes. Probing can find things the model isn't actually using; attribution methods can be noisy; causal interventions can knock the model off-distribution. So if you can show the same story with a few different methods that have different weaknesses, that's way more convincing than one very polished experiment.

And then there's a meta-level point about speed. Early in a project, I think people often over-invest in rigor too soon. When you're exploring, you want fast, scrappy experiments that give you a lot of bits of information about what's going on, so you can build intuition and figure out what the interesting question even is. Then once you have a hypothesis you actually believe, you shift gears and get really rigorous about trying to prove it to a skeptical reader. Mixing those modes up, being sloppy when you should be rigorous, or being rigorous when you should be exploring, is one of the most common mistakes I see.

Finally, simplicity is underrated. If the simple, dumb method works, that's often a more important result than the fancy method, and you should check it first. A lot of the time the honest finding is "the obvious baseline does about as well," and a strong set of experiments is one that would have surfaced that rather than hidden it.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes exploratory, scrappy work from rigorous testing, but does not distinguish a person's aptitude for exploratory tinkering from their aptitude for designing strong experiments.

r002.rationale: It recommends experiments that clearly distinguish hypotheses, but does not prioritize one decisive test of whether an approach works over accumulating many experiments; it also endorses convergent evidence from multiple methods.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the thing that separates strong experiments from weak ones is mostly whether they're actually set up to change your mind. Like, a lot of people, when they start doing research, will come up with a hypothesis and then design an experiment that will produce a nice-looking result if the hypothesis is true. And that's fine as a first step, but the question I always want to ask is: what does this look like if I'm wrong? If the answer is "it looks basically the same," then you haven't really learned anything, you've just confirmed your priors.

So concretely, I think a good experiment has a few properties. One is that there's a clear thing you're trying to find out, and you can state in advance what result would surprise you. Two, you've thought about the boring explanations. In interpretability this comes up constantly. You find some neuron or some feature that seems to do something cool, and the first question should be: is there a dumb reason this could happen? Is it just a frequency effect, is it just correlation with something trivial, would a random baseline look like this? A surprising number of exciting-seeming results evaporate when you run the obvious control.

Three, and I think this is underrated, the experiment should be cheap and fast to run, at least initially. My general philosophy is that research is mostly about the rate at which you get feedback from reality. If you spend three weeks building elaborate infrastructure before you see your first result, you've probably wasted a lot of that time, because your first result will tell you that your framing was wrong in some way you couldn't have predicted. So I'd much rather someone run a scrappy version in an afternoon, look at the output, get confused, and iterate, than build the perfect thing. You can always make it rigorous later once you know what's actually going on.

And then, relatedly, I think strong experiments have a lot of looking at the data in them. Not just metrics. Actually opening up the examples, reading what the model does, staring at the attention patterns or the activations or whatever it is. Metrics are great for scaling up, but the moment where you really understand something usually comes from going "huh, that's weird" at a specific example. The experiments I've seen go badly are often ones where someone had a clean pipeline producing a number and never asked whether the number meant what they assumed it meant.

The last thing I'd say is that a set of experiments, plural, is stronger than any one of them. Ideally you want several angles that would all be hard to explain unless your story is true. One compelling result is easy to fool yourself with. Three independent-ish lines of evidence pointing the same way, where each one has had its obvious confounds checked, is much more convincing, both to you and to whoever reads the paper afterwards.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts quick, scrappy early experiments with later rigor, but does not distinguish aptitude for exploratory tinkering from aptitude for designing strong scientific experiments.

r002.rationale: The response says a set of experiments with several independent lines of evidence is stronger than one result; it does not prioritize a decisive experiment over accumulating many experiments.

astra-6.text:
I think a strong set of experiments is one where you can explain what you would learn from each possible outcome. If the experiment works, what does that tell you? If it fails, which assumption should you question? If every result leaves you with roughly the same story, you probably haven’t designed a very informative experiment.

I’d start with a concrete hypothesis and ask what else could explain the evidence. Then try to design the smallest experiment that distinguishes those explanations. Often that means working in a simpler setting, checking a baseline, or intervening on the thing you think is responsible rather than just observing a correlation.

And I wouldn’t plan the entire sequence in advance. You run something, notice a surprising result, and update what you test next. The point is to build understanding. A failed experiment that exposes a flaw in your mental model can be much more valuable than a successful experiment that confirms something you already expected.

r001.rationale: The response discusses designing informative experiments, but it does not distinguish exploratory tinkering from aptitude for strong scientific experiment design.

r002.rationale: It recommends small experiments that distinguish explanations, but does not clearly prioritize a decisive test of whether an approach works over accumulating many experiments.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a strong set of experiments is one where you can actually learn something whichever way the results go. Before running an experiment, I want to ask: what are my competing hypotheses, what would each predict, and what result would make me change my mind?

It’s easy to have a story you’re excited about, run an experiment, get a result that looks vaguely consistent with it, and feel like you’ve made progress. But often there are several other explanations that would predict the same thing. So a lot of the work is finding a simple test that distinguishes those explanations.

In interpretability, for example, if I think some component of a model is doing a particular job, observing that it activates on relevant examples is a useful starting point. But I’d also want to intervene on it, check whether the model’s behaviour changes as predicted, and look for cases where my explanation breaks down.

And I’d generally rather start with a small, cheap experiment that exposes a flaw in my thinking than build a giant experimental setup around an assumption I haven’t tested.

r001.rationale: The response discusses experiment design and testing explanations, but it does not distinguish skill at exploratory tinkering from skill at designing strong scientific experiments.

r002.rationale: It favors a small, informative test over a large setup, but does not recommend prioritizing one decisive test of whether an approach works over accumulating many experiments.
